extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature, moral philosophy, and leadership; interested general readers of Carlyle's lectures
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards and evaluative principles Carlyle uses when describing or judging 'Heroes' (their character, conduct, and social function), with attention to qualities he praises or condemns. Applicable to literary criticism, moral appraisal, and leadership theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm strength (not mere vehemence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is not strong because he exhibits convulsive vehemence; true strength is 'He that can walk under the heaviest weight without staggering.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle contrasts spasmodic intensity with calm, sustained force: shouting, convulsions, or rigid vehemence are not signs of greatness. The truly strong preserve composure through difficulty and act with steady endurance. (See Rousseau: intense rather than strong; a fundamental mistake to call vehemence and rigidity strength.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent of silence / restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'talent of Silence' is invaluable; the suffering man ought 'to consume his own smoke' rather than emit smoke before it is fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence and self-restraint are virtues of great men: wait for the right time to speak or act. Carlyle criticizes those who cannot 'hold their peace' and equates premature outcry with weakness or lack of deliberation (notably applied to Rousseau and a broader French tendency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnestness (being 'in earnest')
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and chief characteristic of a Hero is being heartily 'in earnest' — a true, driving seriousness of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when other faults exist, earnestness marks a heroic nature. Carlyle notes that earnestness may overrun a weak nature (leading to incoherence or fanaticism), but it remains the central quality that distinguishes a true Hero from mere theorists or dilettantes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming egoism / mastery of desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Egoism is 'the source and summary of all faults and miseries'; a Hero must 'perfect himself into victory over mere Desire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity and hunger for praise corrupt a man's heroism (examples: Rousseau's craving for applause). Moral greatness requires self-command and freedom from petty personal hungers that distort motives and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance and hope for the imperfectly realized Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: One should have tolerance for a man and hope of him; leave him to try what he will do while life lasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle urges charitable interpretation of errors and perversities, framing them as the faltering gestures of a man sent on an errand too big for his nature. The critic or society should allow room for development and transformation rather than immediate condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and truthfulness in life and art
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief quality exemplified by Burns: sincerity — the song 'is not of fantasticalities; it is of a thing felt, really there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True poetry and heroic expression arise from genuine feeling and truth, not from artificiality or operatic 'rose-pink' sensuality. Carlyle contrasts the authentic 'True' with the 'Sham-True' pervasive in his age; sincerity is the moral and aesthetic measure of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and rustic genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble rough genuineness; homely, rustic, honest; true simplicity of strength (as in Burns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength rooted in common life — sturdy, generous, elemental qualities — is admirable. Such robustness combines passion and pity, mirth and hope, and underlies an original mind and authentic expression even when formal culture is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression / substantive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued quality: 'He spoke rather little than much... and always when he did speak, it was to throw new light on the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise speech that contributes insight is superior to loquacity. Carlyle praises speakers who reserve words until they can add real illumination — a standard for rhetorical and literary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: The leader as embodiment of multiple heroic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commander over Men (King) is 'practically the summary for us of all the various figures of Heroism' — priest, teacher, regulator all embodied in the Able-man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle defines kingship/leadership as the convergence of moral, spiritual, and practical authority. A true leader performs the functions of guidance, instruction, and regulation; the office aggregates every heroic dimension into public command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of the Ableman: competence and moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the Ablest Man and raise him to supreme place; he must be the truest-hearted, justest, noblest — what he tells us to do 'must be precisely the wisest, fittest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social procedures (elections, reforms) should aim at elevating genuine ability and moral worth. The quality of governance depends primarily on placing a truly able and virtuous person in authority; all procedural machinery is secondary to this moral selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral legitimacy of authority (Divine Right or Diabolic Wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every claim one man makes upon another there is either a 'Divine Right' or a 'Diabolic Wrong'; obedience is a moral act with a God's-sanction or its violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle recovers a normative dimension to rule: legitimacy is not merely legal or procedural but moral/spiritual. Those who demand obedience without rightful claim or who refuse rightful obedience incur moral blame; rulers must possess moral sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideals as necessary measuring-plumb; approximate rather than perfect embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals exist; if they be not approximated to at all, 'the whole matter goes to wreck.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards and ideals (the plummet/level metaphor) must guide practice. Perfection is unattainable, yet approximating to ideals is essential to prevent social and moral collapse. Ideals function as necessary standards for judgment and reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of unfit or quack leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting the 'too UnAble Man at the head of affairs' causes administrative failure and social eruption — 'quack' rulers produce fermenting masses of misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle warns that false simulacra of ability produce systemic failure: misrule, disorder, revolution. This is a cautionary criterion for evaluating leaders and institutions: competence and moral capacity are non-negotiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship (reverence for Heroes) as social necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero-worship is 'inexpressibly precious' and 'the most solacing fact' for management of the world; certainty that Heroes will be sent and that we can reverence them is a polestar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle regards organized reverence for heroes as a stabilizing and hopeful social force in times of upheaval. The practice of hero-worship channels popular energy towards exemplars and sustains communal orientation amid revolution and doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Heroes requires a sympathetic soul
rubrics_metrics.description: No man can be a 'Grand-Monarque' to his valet-de-chambre; 'The Valet does not know a Hero when he sees him!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception and appreciation of greatness demand a certain moral or aesthetic capacity in the admirer. Carlyle uses this to explain Boswell's reverence for Johnson and to critique those who fail to perceive excellence; sensitivity and depth of response are themselves evaluative criteria.
